content_html:
Are Information and Entropy Consciously Accessible?

Information and entropy are abstract, formal constructs.
The brain likely implements implicit computations that correlate with these constructs (prediction error, uncertainty, efficient codes).
Humans can be conceptually aware (after learning) and phenomenologically aware of related feelings (surprise/confidence), but there’s no native 'entropy qualia.'

The brain does not natively represent “entropy” or “mutual information” as explicit, introspectable variables. Those are scientist‑defined constructs. But neural systems behave as if tracking related quantities—uncertainty, surprise, prediction error—and adjust processing accordingly. People can become conceptually aware of information/entropy via education, and they are often phenomenologically aware of uncertainty or surprise.

Subpersonal computations (not consciously accessible)

  • Efficient coding & predictive processing: Early sensory coding approximates information‑theoretic objectives (decorrelation, redundancy reduction) and predictive error minimization.
  • Surprise & P300/MMN: Deviance and surprise elicit robust EEG/MEG components (P3, MMN) even without attention, indicating preconscious computations.
  • Arousal/uncertainty linkage: Pupil dilations and LC‑NE activity scale with uncertainty and control state, again below explicit awareness.

Conscious metacognition (sometimes accessible)

  • Confidence & volatility judgments: Regions like ACC/medial PFC track uncertainty/volatility; humans can report confidence, though reports dissociate from underlying signals.
  • Learning the concepts: With training, people reason about information/entropy (Shannon), but the phenomenology is still of uncertainty/surprise—not “entropy meters.”

Don’t confuse measures with experiences

Entropy of neural signals is a researcher’s metric (e.g., signal diversity correlates with conscious state), not necessarily something the brain explicitly “feels.”

From abstract quantity to felt experience

Quantity (formal) Conscious feel (typical) Neural signatures Example paradigm
Prediction error / surprise “That was unexpected.” P300 (P3a/P3b), Mismatch Negativity; transient LC–NE and pupil dilation. Oddball/deviant detection; narrative event changes.
Uncertainty / volatility Low confidence; vigilance shifts. ACC/medial PFC signals; pupil/LC–NE scaling; adaptive gain changes. Probabilistic learning with changing contingencies.
Entropy / information rate in input Sensation of complexity/richness (indirect). Efficient coding features; changes in neural signal diversity (MEG/EEG). Naturalistic stimuli vs. controlled regularities.
Boundary strength (event segmentation) Chapter break; “new scene.” Hippocampal boundary peaks; within‑event > across‑boundary linkage. Film/story segmentation; goal/scene/actor switches.

Back to event boundaries — why it can feel like “surprise”

  • Mechanistic link: Event boundaries arise when prediction errors spike and the current event model resets; this overlaps with signatures of surprise, explaining why boundaries often feel like surprises without any explicit sense of “entropy.”
  • Memory consequence: The reset weakens cross‑boundary associations but strengthens within‑event binding—consistent with subjective “chapter breaks.”
